newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends US mixed, retreats from new top vs mark.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends US mixed, retreats from new top vs mark.

text.p: Dollar/yen ended higher but dollar/mark's rally was cut short after setting a new 71-month high in Europe in the wake of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks on Tuesday.
Mark cross activity dominated trade in New York with the German unit firming against the yen and EMS currencies, aiding dollar/yen and weighing on dollar/mark, traders said.

"Ahead of the Bundesbank and Swiss National Bank meetings tomorrow I think prudence would say you take some profits on short mark positions," said Stephen Flanagan, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Credit Agricole Indosuez.

Dollar/mark topped 1.83 for the first time since August 1991, cheered on by buoyant U.S. financial markets after Greenspan delivered the first part of his two-day Congressional testimony on the economy.

"The overnight markets tended to focus more on the fact that bonds and stocks in the U.S. rallied on the remarks, and that the U.S. economy is the best of all possible worlds -- sustainable growth and low inflation," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
The dollar closed at 1.8255/65 marks, off from Europe's high of 1.8325 and 1.8280/90 marks at the open.
The dollar ended at 115.62/72 yen, up from 115.10/20.

More subdued U.S. asset markets offered less support for the dollar than on Tuesday, when the Dow industrials jumped nearly 155 points and bond yields fell to their lowest level in almost eight months, traders said.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 1/4 point and the Dow ended up a relatively tame 26.71 points.

Greenspan continued his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday. But the address had little impact on trade, being mostly a rehash of the previous day's remarks to the House.
The dollar came under some pressure after Fed vice chair Alice Rivlin said the dollar may not get much stronger.
Traders said they were unsure how to interpret her remarks, which could have also been construed as an endorsement of a strong dollar.
Rivlin told legislators on Wednesday that the strength of the U.S. dollar had helped to keep import prices in check but that the currency was unlikely to race ahead much further.
"I'm not sure that what she said was considered new information from her," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange Trading manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.
"Keep in mind that dollar commentary is not in the Fed's purview, anyway," Pettit added.

Mark/yen rose retraced most of its earlier slide to two-year low at 62.93, ending near 63.35. Sterling/mark backed off a bit more after powering to a more than seven-year high at 3.0878 in early trade.
In other trade, the dollar was unchaged at 1.4850/60 Swiss francs and rose to Canadian $1.3821/26 from C$1.3766/71.
The Australian dollar was steady at $0.7360/65, compared to $0.7361/66. ((-- Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
